blocks.text: Damascus is not merely a name attached to Saul’s encounter. The city belonged to a concrete landscape shaped by Levantine travel routes, imperial borders, settled communities, water access, trade, and neighboring peoples. Acts therefore places Saul’s journey, helpless arrival, and first preaching within a connected urban setting rather than an isolated wilderness scene.

Acts portrays Saul’s call as a sequence involving bodily incapacity and dependence: he cannot see, must be led by others, fasts for three days, receives Ananias’s touch, regains his sight, is baptized, eats, and begins his mission. This allows dependency and care to remain part of the account rather than treating them as incidental obstacles. It does not, however, establish that this blindness was Paul’s later “thorn” or provide a diagnosis for every hardship mentioned in his letters; illness, injury, deprivation, violence, and imprisonment should remain distinct categories.

Acts and Galatians select and arrange Paul’s call and Jerusalem contacts differently. Acts gives a later, continuous narrative, while Galatians presents selective first-person intervals for its own purposes. Exact harmonization remains disputed, so neither automatic agreement nor automatic contradiction should replace passage-by-passage comparison; Acts should not be treated as a verbatim transcript, and every Jerusalem visit need not be assigned with certainty.

The encounter may be described as conversion, prophetic call, or commissioning, but these labels overlap and their precise relationship is debated. Acts itself recounts Paul’s encounter three times with rhetorical differences, so the presentation in chapter 9 should be read as this narrative’s particular telling rather than as the only possible wording or emphasis.

First Corinthians 15 offers another early account relevant to Paul’s appearance claim: it transmits a sequence of Jesus’ death, burial, resurrection, and appearances, culminating in an appearance to Paul. That testimony should remain distinct from Acts 9’s fuller narrative of light, blindness, Ananias, baptism, and ensuing mission rather than having the details of one account silently imported into the other.

Tabitha is explicitly called a disciple, and the widows’ display of garments makes her practical work within the community visible. Her portrayal fits Acts’ broader presentation of women as disciples, patrons, hosts, teachers, workers, converts, and sufferers, although that presentation remains selective and reflects continuing patriarchal constraints.

sections.title: The Text and Historical Evaluation of Acts

blocks.text: Acts is preserved in early papyri and major Greek codices, including P45, P53, P74, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, and Bezae, which preserve different portions and textual profiles. Codex Bezae and related witnesses contain a substantially distinctive form often called the Western text, but its individual readings require case-by-case judgment. Historical evaluation likewise works best claim by claim through comparison with independent evidence, rather than by declaring Acts uniformly reliable or unreliable.
